points.title: Earnings-per-share growth-rate test (5 year vs 10 year)
points.question: A test for determining the earnings per share growth rate. For earnings to grow, the company must employ its retained earnings in a manner that will generate more earnings per share. The increase in per share earnings will, over time, increase the price of the share. Mathematical method: figure the annual compounded rate of growth of per share earnings for the last ten years (long term) and the last five years (short term). If, for example, long term is 12% and short term is 16%, the company has had a higher rate of return of earnings growth in the last five years than in the ten year period. What were the business economics that caused this change? Is the company buying up its stock? Finding new business ventures? Note: to adapt the per share growth rate to negative earnings, simply start back one year. You should never use fewer than seven years.

points.title: Actively buying back its shares
points.question: Is the company actively buying back its shares? The repurchasing of shares is one of Warren's favourite tricks to increase his ownership in a company without having to invest any more of his own money. Take the number of shares outstanding ten years ago, subtract from it the number of shares outstanding in the current year, and you get the number of shares the company has purchased over the last ten years. A negative number indicates the number of shares that the company has added. Warren is looking for a decrease in the number of shares outstanding.

points.title: Can the company repurchase shares to investors' advantage?
points.question: A good sign that a company has a DCA is that it will have a long history of buying back its shares. To buy back shares over a number of years, a company needs an abundance of free cash. Companies with DCA have the economic power to earn the money they need to implement a long term share repurchase programme. Price competitive businesses seldom have the excess capital necessary to buy back shares. Instead the reverse happens: they issue more shares to raise new money to support their cash hungry businesses.

points.title: Can the company increase prices along with inflation?
points.question: Can the company increase prices along with inflation? It might not be a great wealth building tool, but a company with a DCA offers an increase in value right along with inflation. An interesting question that requires investigative work. If the company's product is selling at the same price as twenty years ago, then you are most likely dealing with a commodity business and should give it a pass. If the price of the product has risen on an average of at least 4% a year over the last twenty years, then you can bet the farm that it's the kind of business that can raise prices along with inflation. Financial equation for use with TI BA-35 Solar calculator: company's ability to raise prices with inflation. Use the price of the product twenty years ago as your present value (PV), the current price of the product as your future value (FV), and 20 as your number of years (N). Hit compute (CPT) then the interest key (i) and your annual compounding growth rate in price will be calculated. (If you get a negative number, it means you are probably looking at a price-competitive business and should move on.)

points.title: Right operational costs (low maintenance capex)
points.question: Does the company have right operational costs? The more durable a competitive advantage, the less a business has to spend to maintain it. A simple mathematical formula is to take the amount of earnings retained by a business for a certain period and measure its effect on the earning capacity of the company. With DCA, retained earnings are either used to expand operations, invest in new businesses and/or repurchases - all three should have a positive effect on per share earnings. Are large capital expenditures required to update plant and equipment? If they are building cars or designing software, they may not have to buy big expensive jets, or can use the same equipment for twenty years without any risk of obsolescence. If the answer is yes, be careful.

points.title: Market panic, business recession or curable individual calamity
points.question: Is the company's stock price suffering from a market panic, a business recession, or an individual calamity that is curable? As we discussed, these types of situations usually offer the best prices. If you can't buy during one of these events, then you are probably paying full price for the stock. If you want to get rich, you have to learn how to exploit a bad-news situation and the stock market's shortsightedness.

points.title: Initial rate of return vs US Treasury bonds
points.question: What is the initial rate of return on the investment and how does it compare to the return on U.S. treasury bonds? The price you pay to BUY determines your rate of return - pay less, earn more; pay more, earn less. Take the company's current per share earnings and divide it by the current price of a single share. This will give you the investment's initial rate of return. Then compare the investment's initial rate of return and expected growth rate per share to the return being paid on U.S. treasury bonds. If the treasuries look juicier, the stock might be overpriced.

Relative Value = Per Share Earnings / Current Treasury Bond Return.

points.title: Projected annual compounding return as an equity/bond (Book Value model)
points.question: What is the company's projected annual compounding return as an equity/bond? Take the company's average per share return on equity for the last ten years and subtract the average percentage that is not retained and is paid out as a dividend. Use the resulting difference as the rate of growth that the company's book value will grow. Use the company's book value in the current year as the present value (PV), and use the calculated rate of growth for book value as the rate of interest (i). Punch in 10 for the number of years out that you want to make your projection (N), then hit the CPT key, followed by the future-value key (FV). This will calculate the per share book value of the company ten years out. To determine the selling price of the company's stock ten years out, take the company's future per share book value and multiply it by the average return on equity - this gives the company's projected per share earnings. Then multiply the projected earnings by the company's average annual P/E ratio for the last ten years - this gives the company's projected per share future trading price. Using the company's current market price as your present value (PV) and the projected future trading price as the future value (FV) and the number of years between the two (N), hit CPT and then the i key, which calculates the projected annual compounding return that the investment will produce.

points.title: Projected return using historical per-share earnings growth / Intrinsic Value
points.question: What is the projected annual compounding return using the historical annual per share earnings growth? To calculate the projected annual compounding return on an investment purchased in 2002 and sold during 2012, first determine the annual compounding per share growth from 1992 to 2002. Then, using the 1992 to 2002 per share growth rate, project forward the company's per share earnings to 2012 and multiply it by the average annual P/E ratio for 1992 to 2002. This will give you the projected trading price of the stock in 2012. Use the 1992 per share earnings as the present value (PV), 2002 per share earnings as the future value (FV) and 10 for the number of years (N), hit CPT and the i key to get the company's per share annual compounding growth rate. Now use the 2002 per share earnings as PV, that growth rate as i, and 10 years - hit CPT then FV - to get the projected per share earnings for 2012. Multiply by the average P/E ratio to get the projected trading price.

points.title: Durable Competitive Advantage
points.question: Does the company have an identifiable durable competitive advantage? If yes, describe it in as simple a manner as you can, as you would to a seven-year-old child. Warren likes to keep things simple. If you can't explain it to a child, then the durable competitive advantage probably doesn't exist. If you can't find a durable competitive advantage, keep your powder dry until you do. Waiting for the perfect pitch never bothered Warren.

points.title: Brand-name product or key service
points.question: Does the company have a brand name product or service that gives it a competitive advantage? If 6, 7, 5.2, 8 are a yes, then you need to find out whether it is selling a product or service that has a durable competitive advantage. Does it sell a brand-name product or a key service that people or businesses are dependent on? Products are much easier to identify than services, so start with them. Ask yourself: Is the product the kind that stores have to carry to be in business? Would the businesses that carry this kind of product be losing sales if they didn't carry this particular brand-name product? If you remember your parents using it, drinking it, smoking it or doing something else with it, it is usually a good sign. Ask a pharmacist or a car mechanic - related people - they can tell how it sold and how it sells. Better if it's a CRAP. Companies providing services that have durable competitive advantages are much harder to identify. Look to the economics of the business: is the company's service necessary for businesses that use it to stay in business? If the service is aimed at individual consumers, ask whether consumers are constantly in need of it. As in the world of products, the frequency of the consumer's need differentiates the quality of the competitive advantage.

points.title: Predicting earnings at a glance (Company I / II / III / IV)
points.question: One will confront four types of companies, among them three interest us. Company 1: in a perfect situation, a company's per share earnings are consistently A) Strong and B) Show an upward trend. Company 2: might have some investment merit, but from a Buffett point of view, the lack of strong earnings indicates that future earnings would be impossible to predict. Company 3: shows a substantially weaker performance in the latest year than the year before. Company 4: shows an actual loss. Is the condition permanent or is it something that management or the economic environment can correct over time?

points.title: Earnings-per-share growth-rate test (5 year vs 10 year)
points.question: A test for determining the earnings per share growth rate. For earnings to grow, the company must employ its retained earnings in a manner that will generate more earnings per share. The increase in per share earnings will, over time, increase the price of the share. Mathematical method: figure the annual compounded rate of growth of per share earnings for the last ten years (long term) and the last five years (short term). If, for example, long term is 12% and short term is 16%, the company has had a higher rate of return of earnings growth in the last five years than in the ten year period. What were the business economics that caused this change? Is the company buying up its stock? Finding new business ventures? Note: to adapt the per share growth rate to negative earnings, simply start back one year. You should never use fewer than seven years.

points.title: Actively buying back its shares
points.question: Is the company actively buying back its shares? The repurchasing of shares is one of Warren's favourite tricks to increase his ownership in a company without having to invest any more of his own money. Take the number of shares outstanding ten years ago, subtract from it the number of shares outstanding in the current year, and you get the number of shares the company has purchased over the last ten years. A negative number indicates the number of shares that the company has added. Warren is looking for a decrease in the number of shares outstanding.

points.title: Can the company repurchase shares to investors' advantage?
points.question: A good sign that a company has a DCA is that it will have a long history of buying back its shares. To buy back shares over a number of years, a company needs an abundance of free cash. Companies with DCA have the economic power to earn the money they need to implement a long term share repurchase programme. Price competitive businesses seldom have the excess capital necessary to buy back shares. Instead the reverse happens: they issue more shares to raise new money to support their cash hungry businesses.

points.title: Can the company increase prices along with inflation?
points.question: Can the company increase prices along with inflation? It might not be a great wealth building tool, but a company with a DCA offers an increase in value right along with inflation. An interesting question that requires investigative work. If the company's product is selling at the same price as twenty years ago, then you are most likely dealing with a commodity business and should give it a pass. If the price of the product has risen on an average of at least 4% a year over the last twenty years, then you can bet the farm that it's the kind of business that can raise prices along with inflation. Financial equation for use with TI BA-35 Solar calculator: company's ability to raise prices with inflation. Use the price of the product twenty years ago as your present value (PV), the current price of the product as your future value (FV), and 20 as your number of years (N). Hit compute (CPT) then the interest key (i) and your annual compounding growth rate in price will be calculated. (If you get a negative number, it means you are probably looking at a price-competitive business and should move on.)

points.title: Right operational costs (low maintenance capex)
points.question: Does the company have right operational costs? The more durable a competitive advantage, the less a business has to spend to maintain it. A simple mathematical formula is to take the amount of earnings retained by a business for a certain period and measure its effect on the earning capacity of the company. With DCA, retained earnings are either used to expand operations, invest in new businesses and/or repurchases - all three should have a positive effect on per share earnings. Are large capital expenditures required to update plant and equipment? If they are building cars or designing software, they may not have to buy big expensive jets, or can use the same equipment for twenty years without any risk of obsolescence. If the answer is yes, be careful.

points.title: Market panic, business recession or curable individual calamity
points.question: Is the company's stock price suffering from a market panic, a business recession, or an individual calamity that is curable? As we discussed, these types of situations usually offer the best prices. If you can't buy during one of these events, then you are probably paying full price for the stock. If you want to get rich, you have to learn how to exploit a bad-news situation and the stock market's shortsightedness.

points.title: Initial rate of return vs US Treasury bonds
points.question: What is the initial rate of return on the investment and how does it compare to the return on U.S. treasury bonds? The price you pay to BUY determines your rate of return - pay less, earn more; pay more, earn less. Take the company's current per share earnings and divide it by the current price of a single share. This will give you the investment's initial rate of return. Then compare the investment's initial rate of return and expected growth rate per share to the return being paid on U.S. treasury bonds. If the treasuries look juicier, the stock might be overpriced.

points.question: A stock's value relative to treasury bonds: all investments compete with one another but the return on treasury bonds is the benchmark that all investments must ultimately compete with. To establish the value of the company relative to treasury bonds, divide the current per share earnings by the current return on treasury bonds. Relative Value = Per Share Earnings / Current Treasury Bond Return.

points.title: Projected annual compounding return as an equity/bond (Book Value model)
points.question: What is the company's projected annual compounding return as an equity/bond? Take the company's average per share return on equity for the last ten years and subtract the average percentage that is not retained and is paid out as a dividend. Use the resulting difference as the rate of growth that the company's book value will grow. Use the company's book value in the current year as the present value (PV), and use the calculated rate of growth for book value as the rate of interest (i). Punch in 10 for the number of years out that you want to make your projection (N), then hit the CPT key, followed by the future-value key (FV). This will calculate the per share book value of the company ten years out. To determine the selling price of the company's stock ten years out, take the company's future per share book value and multiply it by the average return on equity - this gives the company's projected per share earnings. Then multiply the projected earnings by the company's average annual P/E ratio for the last ten years - this gives the company's projected per share future trading price. Using the company's current market price as your present value (PV) and the projected future trading price as the future value (FV) and the number of years between the two (N), hit CPT and then the i key, which calculates the projected annual compounding return that the investment will produce.

points.title: Projected return using historical per-share earnings growth / Intrinsic Value
points.question: What is the projected annual compounding return using the historical annual per share earnings growth? To calculate the projected annual compounding return on an investment purchased in 2002 and sold during 2012, first determine the annual compounding per share growth from 1992 to 2002. Then, using the 1992 to 2002 per share growth rate, project forward the company's per share earnings to 2012 and multiply it by the average annual P/E ratio for 1992 to 2002. This will give you the projected trading price of the stock in 2012. Use the 1992 per share earnings as the present value (PV), 2002 per share earnings as the future value (FV) and 10 for the number of years (N), hit CPT and the i key to get the company's per share annual compounding growth rate. Now use the 2002 per share earnings as PV, that growth rate as i, and 10 years - hit CPT then FV - to get the projected per share earnings for 2012. Multiply by the average P/E ratio to get the projected trading price.

points.question: Does the company have an identifiable durable competitive advantage? If yes, describe it in as simple a manner as you can, as you would to a seven-year-old child. If you can't find a durable competitive advantage, keep your powder dry until you do. Waiting for the perfect pitch never bothered Warren.

points.title: Brand-name product or key service
points.question: Does the company have a brand name product or service that gives it a competitive advantage? If 6, 7, 5.2, 8 are a yes, then you need to find out whether it is selling a product or service that has a durable competitive advantage. Does it sell a brand-name product or a key service that people or businesses are dependent on? Products are much easier to identify than services, so start with them. Ask yourself: Is the product the kind that stores have to carry to be in business? If the service is aimed at individual consumers, ask whether consumers are constantly in need of it. As in the world of products, the frequency of the consumer's need differentiates the quality of the competitive advantage.

points.title: Predicting earnings at a glance (Company I / II / III / IV)

Is the condition permanent or is it something that management or the economic environment can correct over time?

points.title: Earnings-per-share growth-rate test (5 year vs 10 year)
points.question: A test for determining the earnings per share growth rate. For earnings to grow, the company must employ its retained earnings in a manner that will generate more earnings per share. The increase in per share earnings will, over time, increase the price of the share. Mathematical method: figure the annual compounded rate of growth of per share earnings for the last ten years (long term) and the last five years (short term). If, for example, long term is 12% and short term is 16%, the company has had a higher rate of return of earnings growth in the last five years than in the ten year period. What were the business economics that caused this change? Is the company buying up its stock? Finding new business ventures? Note: to adapt the per share growth rate to negative earnings, simply start back one year. You should never use fewer than seven years.

points.title: Actively buying back its shares
points.question: Is the company actively buying back its shares? The repurchasing of shares is one of Warren's favourite tricks to increase his ownership in a company without having to invest any more of his own money. Take the number of shares outstanding ten years ago, subtract from it the number of shares outstanding in the current year, and you get the number of shares the company has purchased over the last ten years. A negative number indicates the number of shares that the company has added. Warren is looking for a decrease in the number of shares outstanding.

points.title: Can the company repurchase shares to investors' advantage?
points.question: A good sign that a company has a DCA is that it will have a long history of buying back its shares. To buy back shares over a number of years, a company needs an abundance of free cash. Companies with DCA have the economic power to earn the money they need to implement a long term share repurchase programme. Price competitive businesses seldom have the excess capital necessary to buy back shares. Instead the reverse happens: they issue more shares to raise new money to support their cash hungry businesses.

points.title: Can the company increase prices along with inflation?
points.question: Can the company increase prices along with inflation? It might not be a great wealth building tool, but a company with a DCA offers an increase in value right along with inflation. An interesting question that requires investigative work. If the company's product is selling at the same price as twenty years ago, then you are most likely dealing with a commodity business and should give it a pass. If the price of the product has risen on an average of at least 4% a year over the last twenty years, then you can bet the farm that it's the kind of business that can raise prices along with inflation. Financial equation for use with TI BA-35 Solar calculator: company's ability to raise prices with inflation. Use the price of the product twenty years ago as your present value (PV), the current price of the product as your future value (FV), and 20 as your number of years (N). Hit compute (CPT) then the interest key (i) and your annual compounding growth rate in price will be calculated. (If you get a negative number, it means you are probably looking at a price-competitive business and should move on.)

points.title: Right operational costs (low maintenance capex)
points.question: Does the company have right operational costs? The more durable a competitive advantage, the less a business has to spend to maintain it. A simple mathematical formula is to take the amount of earnings retained by a business for a certain period and measure its effect on the earning capacity of the company. With DCA, retained earnings are either used to expand operations, invest in new businesses and/or repurchases - all three should have a positive effect on per share earnings. Are large capital expenditures required to update plant and equipment? If they are building cars or designing software, they may not have to buy big expensive jets, or can use the same equipment for twenty years without any risk of obsolescence. If the answer is yes, be careful.

points.question: Is the company's stock price suffering from a market panic, a business recession, or an individual calamity that is curable? As we discussed, these types of situations usually offer the best prices. If you can't buy during one of these events, then you are probably paying full price for the stock. If you want to get rich, you have to learn how to exploit a bad-news situation and the stock market's shortsightedness.

points.title: Initial rate of return vs US Treasury bonds
points.question: What is the initial rate of return on the investment and how does it compare to the return on U.S. treasury bonds? The price you pay to BUY determines your rate of return - pay less, earn more; pay more, earn less. Take the company's current per share earnings and divide it by the current price of a single share. This will give you the investment's initial rate of return. Then compare the investment's initial rate of return and expected growth rate per share to the return being paid on U.S. treasury bonds. If the treasuries look juicier, the stock might be overpriced.

Relative Value = Per Share Earnings / Current Treasury Bond Return.

points.title: Projected annual compounding return as an equity/bond (Book Value model)
points.question: What is the company's projected annual compounding return as an equity/bond? Take the company's average per share return on equity for the last ten years and subtract the average percentage that is not retained and is paid out as a dividend. Use the resulting difference as the rate of growth that the company's book value will grow. Use the company's book value in the current year as the present value (PV), and use the calculated rate of growth for book value as the rate of interest (i). Punch in 10 for the number of years out that you want to make your projection (N), then hit the CPT key, followed by the future-value key (FV). This will calculate the per share book value of the company ten years out. To determine the selling price of the company's stock ten years out, take the company's future per share book value and multiply it by the average return on equity - this gives the company's projected per share earnings. Then multiply the projected earnings by the company's average annual P/E ratio for the last ten years - this gives the company's projected per share future trading price. Using the company's current market price as your present value (PV) and the projected future trading price as the future value (FV) and the number of years between the two (N), hit CPT and then the i key, which calculates the projected annual compounding return that the investment will produce.

Then multiply the projected earnings by the company's average annual P/E ratio for the last ten years - this gives the company's projected per share future trading price. Using the company's current market price as your present value (PV) and the projected future trading price as the future value (FV) and the number of years between the two (N), hit CPT and then the i key, which calculates the projected annual compounding return that the investment will produce.

points.title: Projected return using historical per-share earnings growth / Intrinsic Value
points.question: What is the projected annual compounding return using the historical annual per share earnings growth? To calculate the projected annual compounding return on an investment purchased in 2002 and sold during 2012, first determine the annual compounding per share growth from 1992 to 2002. Then, using the 1992 to 2002 per share growth rate, project forward the company's per share earnings to 2012 and multiply it by the average annual P/E ratio for 1992 to 2002. This will give you the projected trading price of the stock in 2012. Use the 1992 per share earnings as the present value (PV), 2002 per share earnings as the future value (FV) and 10 for the number of years (N), hit CPT and the i key to get the company's per share annual compounding growth rate. Now use the 2002 per share earnings as PV, that growth rate as i, and 10 years - hit CPT then FV - to get the projected per share earnings for 2012. Multiply by the average P/E ratio to get the projected trading price.

points.question: Does the company have an identifiable durable competitive advantage? If yes, describe it in as simple a manner as you can, as you would to a seven-year-old child. Warren likes to keep things simple. If you can't explain it to a child, then the durable competitive advantage probably doesn't exist. If you can't find a durable competitive advantage, keep your powder dry until you do. Waiting for the perfect pitch never bothered Warren.

points.title: Brand-name product or key service
points.question: Does the company have a brand name product or service that gives it a competitive advantage? If 6, 7, 5.2, 8 are a yes, then you need to find out whether it is selling a product or service that has a durable competitive advantage. Does it sell a brand-name product or a key service that people or businesses are dependent on? Products are much easier to identify than services, so start with them. Ask yourself: Is the product the kind that stores have to carry to be in business? Would the businesses that carry this kind of product be losing sales if they didn't carry this particular brand-name product? If you remember your parents using it, drinking it, smoking it or doing something else with it, it is usually a good sign. Ask a pharmacist or a car mechanic - related people - they can tell how it sold and how it sells. Better if it's a CRAP. Companies providing services that have durable competitive advantages are much harder to identify. Look to the economics of the business: is the company's service necessary for businesses that use it to stay in business? If the service is aimed at individual consumers, ask whether consumers are constantly in need of it. As in the world of products, the frequency of the consumer's need differentiates the quality of the competitive advantage.

points.title: Predicting earnings at a glance (Company I / II / III / IV)
points.question: One will confront four types of companies, among them three interest us. Company 1: in a perfect situation, a company's per share earnings are consistently A) Strong and B) Show an upward trend. Company 3: shows a substantially weaker performance in the latest year than the year before. Company 4: shows an actual loss. Is the condition permanent or is it something that management or the economic environment can correct over time?

points.title: Earnings-per-share growth-rate test (5 year vs 10 year)
points.question: A test for determining the earnings per share growth rate. For earnings to grow, the company must employ its retained earnings in a manner that will generate more earnings per share. The increase in per share earnings will, over time, increase the price of the share. Mathematical method: figure the annual compounded rate of growth of per share earnings for the last ten years (long term) and the last five years (short term). If, for example, long term is 12% and short term is 16%, the company has had a higher rate of return of earnings growth in the last five years than in the ten year period. What were the business economics that caused this change? Is the company buying up its stock? Finding new business ventures? Note: to adapt the per share growth rate to negative earnings, simply start back one year. You should never use fewer than seven years.

points.title: Actively buying back its shares
points.question: Is the company actively buying back its shares? The repurchasing of shares is one of Warren's favourite tricks to increase his ownership in a company without having to invest any more of his own money. Take the number of shares outstanding ten years ago, subtract from it the number of shares outstanding in the current year, and you get the number of shares the company has purchased over the last ten years. A negative number indicates the number of shares that the company has added. Warren is looking for a decrease in the number of shares outstanding.

points.title: Can the company repurchase shares to investors' advantage?
points.question: A good sign that a company has a DCA is that it will have a long history of buying back its shares. To buy back shares over a number of years, a company needs an abundance of free cash. Companies with DCA have the economic power to earn the money they need to implement a long term share repurchase programme. Price competitive businesses seldom have the excess capital necessary to buy back shares. Instead the reverse happens: they issue more shares to raise new money to support their cash hungry businesses.

points.title: Can the company increase prices along with inflation?
points.question: Can the company increase prices along with inflation? It might not be a great wealth building tool, but a company with a DCA offers an increase in value right along with inflation. An interesting question that requires investigative work. If the company's product is selling at the same price as twenty years ago, then you are most likely dealing with a commodity business and should give it a pass. If the price of the product has risen on an average of at least 4% a year over the last twenty years, then you can bet the farm that it's the kind of business that can raise prices along with inflation. Financial equation for use with TI BA-35 Solar calculator: company's ability to raise prices with inflation. Use the price of the product twenty years ago as your present value (PV), the current price of the product as your future value (FV), and 20 as your number of years (N). Hit compute (CPT) then the interest key (i) and your annual compounding growth rate in price will be calculated. (If you get a negative number, it means you are probably looking at a price-competitive business and should move on.)

points.title: Right operational costs (low maintenance capex)
points.question: Does the company have right operational costs? The more durable a competitive advantage, the less a business has to spend to maintain it. A simple mathematical formula is to take the amount of earnings retained by a business for a certain period and measure its effect on the earning capacity of the company. With DCA, retained earnings are either used to expand operations, invest in new businesses and/or repurchases - all three should have a positive effect on per share earnings. Are large capital expenditures required to update plant and equipment? If they are building cars or designing software, they may not have to buy big expensive jets, or can use the same equipment for twenty years without any risk of obsolescence. If the answer is yes, be careful.

points.title: Market panic, business recession or curable individual calamity
points.question: Is the company's stock price suffering from a market panic, a business recession, or an individual calamity that is curable? As we discussed, these types of situations usually offer the best prices. If you can't buy during one of these events, then you are probably paying full price for the stock. If you want to get rich, you have to learn how to exploit a bad-news situation and the stock market's shortsightedness.

points.title: Initial rate of return vs US Treasury bonds
points.question: What is the initial rate of return on the investment and how does it compare to the return on U.S. treasury bonds? The price you pay to BUY determines your rate of return - pay less, earn more; pay more, earn less. Take the company's current per share earnings and divide it by the current price of a single share. This will give you the investment's initial rate of return. Then compare the investment's initial rate of return and expected growth rate per share to the return being paid on U.S. treasury bonds. If the treasuries look juicier, the stock might be overpriced.

points.question: A stock's value relative to treasury bonds: all investments compete with one another but the return on treasury bonds is the benchmark that all investments must ultimately compete with. To establish the value of the company relative to treasury bonds, divide the current per share earnings by the current return on treasury bonds. Relative Value = Per Share Earnings / Current Treasury Bond Return.

points.title: Projected annual compounding return as an equity/bond (Book Value model)
points.question: What is the company's projected annual compounding return as an equity/bond? Take the company's average per share return on equity for the last ten years and subtract the average percentage that is not retained and is paid out as a dividend. Use the resulting difference as the rate of growth that the company's book value will grow. Use the company's book value in the current year as the present value (PV), and use the calculated rate of growth for book value as the rate of interest (i). Punch in 10 for the number of years out that you want to make your projection (N), then hit the CPT key, followed by the future-value key (FV). This will calculate the per share book value of the company ten years out. To determine the selling price of the company's stock ten years out, take the company's future per share book value and multiply it by the average return on equity - this gives the company's projected per share earnings. Then multiply the projected earnings by the company's average annual P/E ratio for the last ten years - this gives the company's projected per share future trading price. Using the company's current market price as your present value (PV) and the projected future trading price as the future value (FV) and the number of years between the two (N), hit CPT and then the i key, which calculates the projected annual compounding return that the investment will produce.

points.formula: Book Value Growth % = ROE% * (1 - Payout%/100)  ->  BV in 10Y = BV_now * (1+g)^10  ->  EPS in 10Y = BV_10Y * ROE%/100  ->  Price in 10Y = EPS_10Y * Terminal P/E  ->  Intrinsic Value = Price_Projected_10Y / (1 + r)^10  ->  Compounding return = ((Price_10Y / Price_now)^(1/10) - 1) * 100

points.title: Projected return using historical per-share earnings growth / Intrinsic Value
points.question: What is the projected annual compounding return using the historical annual per share earnings growth? To calculate the projected annual compounding return on an investment purchased in 2002 and sold during 2012, first determine the annual compounding per share growth from 1992 to 2002. Then, using the 1992 to 2002 per share growth rate, project forward the company's per share earnings to 2012 and multiply it by the average annual P/E ratio for 1992 to 2002. This will give you the projected trading price of the stock in 2012. Use the 1992 per share earnings as the present value (PV), 2002 per share earnings as the future value (FV) and 10 for the number of years (N), hit CPT and the i key to get the company's per share annual compounding growth rate. Now use the 2002 per share earnings as PV, that growth rate as i, and 10 years - hit CPT then FV - to get the projected per share earnings for 2012. Multiply by the average P/E ratio to get the projected trading price.

Use the 1992 per share earnings as the present value (PV), 2002 per share earnings as the future value (FV) and 10 for the number of years (N), hit CPT and the i key to get the company's per share annual compounding growth rate. Now use the 2002 per share earnings as PV, that growth rate as i, and 10 years - hit CPT then FV - to get the projected per share earnings for 2012. points.formula: EPS_10Y = EPS_now * (1 + min(EPS CAGR, 18%))^10  ->  Price_10Y = EPS_10Y * Terminal P/E  ->  Intrinsic Value = Price_10Y / (1 + r)^10  ->  Compounding return = ((Price_10Y/P_now)^(1/10)-1)*100

Warren likes to keep things simple. If you can't explain it to a child, then the durable competitive advantage probably doesn't exist. If you can't find a durable competitive advantage, keep your powder dry until you do. Waiting for the perfect pitch never bothered Warren.

points.title: Brand-name product or key service
points.question: Does the company have a brand name product or service that gives it a competitive advantage? If 6, 7, 5.2, 8 are a yes, then you need to find out whether it is selling a product or service that has a durable competitive advantage. Does it sell a brand-name product or a key service that people or businesses are dependent on? Products are much easier to identify than services, so start with them. Ask yourself: Is the product the kind that stores have to carry to be in business? Would the businesses that carry this kind of product be losing sales if they didn't carry this particular brand-name product? If you remember your parents using it, drinking it, smoking it or doing something else with it, it is usually a good sign. Ask a pharmacist or a car mechanic - related people - they can tell how it sold and how it sells. Better if it's a CRAP. Companies providing services that have durable competitive advantages are much harder to identify. Look to the economics of the business: is the company's service necessary for businesses that use it to stay in business? If the service is aimed at individual consumers, ask whether consumers are constantly in need of it. As in the world of products, the frequency of the consumer's need differentiates the quality of the competitive advantage.

points.title: Predicting earnings at a glance (Company I / II / III / IV)
points.question: One will confront four types of companies, among them three interest us. Company 3: shows a substantially weaker performance in the latest year than the year before. Company 4: shows an actual loss. Is the condition permanent or is it something that management or the economic environment can correct over time?

points.title: Earnings-per-share growth-rate test (5 year vs 10 year)
points.question: A test for determining the earnings per share growth rate. For earnings to grow, the company must employ its retained earnings in a manner that will generate more earnings per share. The increase in per share earnings will, over time, increase the price of the share. Mathematical method: figure the annual compounded rate of growth of per share earnings for the last ten years (long term) and the last five years (short term). If, for example, long term is 12% and short term is 16%, the company has had a higher rate of return of earnings growth in the last five years than in the ten year period. What were the business economics that caused this change? Is the company buying up its stock? Finding new business ventures? Note: to adapt the per share growth rate to negative earnings, simply start back one year. You should never use fewer than seven years.

points.title: Actively buying back its shares
points.question: Is the company actively buying back its shares? The repurchasing of shares is one of Warren's favourite tricks to increase his ownership in a company without having to invest any more of his own money. Take the number of shares outstanding ten years ago, subtract from it the number of shares outstanding in the current year, and you get the number of shares the company has purchased over the last ten years. A negative number indicates the number of shares that the company has added. Warren is looking for a decrease in the number of shares outstanding.

points.title: Can the company repurchase shares to investors' advantage?
points.question: A good sign that a company has a DCA is that it will have a long history of buying back its shares. To buy back shares over a number of years, a company needs an abundance of free cash. Companies with DCA have the economic power to earn the money they need to implement a long term share repurchase programme. Price competitive businesses seldom have the excess capital necessary to buy back shares. Instead the reverse happens: they issue more shares to raise new money to support their cash hungry businesses.

points.title: Can the company increase prices along with inflation?
points.question: Can the company increase prices along with inflation? It might not be a great wealth building tool, but a company with a DCA offers an increase in value right along with inflation. An interesting question that requires investigative work. If the company's product is selling at the same price as twenty years ago, then you are most likely dealing with a commodity business and should give it a pass. If the price of the product has risen on an average of at least 4% a year over the last twenty years, then you can bet the farm that it's the kind of business that can raise prices along with inflation. Financial equation for use with TI BA-35 Solar calculator: company's ability to raise prices with inflation. Use the price of the product twenty years ago as your present value (PV), the current price of the product as your future value (FV), and 20 as your number of years (N). Hit compute (CPT) then the interest key (i) and your annual compounding growth rate in price will be calculated. (If you get a negative number, it means you are probably looking at a price-competitive business and should move on.)

points.title: Right operational costs (low maintenance capex)
points.question: Does the company have right operational costs? The more durable a competitive advantage, the less a business has to spend to maintain it. A simple mathematical formula is to take the amount of earnings retained by a business for a certain period and measure its effect on the earning capacity of the company. With DCA, retained earnings are either used to expand operations, invest in new businesses and/or repurchases - all three should have a positive effect on per share earnings. Are large capital expenditures required to update plant and equipment? If they are building cars or designing software, they may not have to buy big expensive jets, or can use the same equipment for twenty years without any risk of obsolescence. If the answer is yes, be careful.

points.title: Market panic, business recession or curable individual calamity
points.question: Is the company's stock price suffering from a market panic, a business recession, or an individual calamity that is curable? As we discussed, these types of situations usually offer the best prices. If you can't buy during one of these events, then you are probably paying full price for the stock. If you want to get rich, you have to learn how to exploit a bad-news situation and the stock market's shortsightedness.

points.title: Initial rate of return vs US Treasury bonds
points.question: What is the initial rate of return on the investment and how does it compare to the return on U.S. treasury bonds? The price you pay to BUY determines your rate of return - pay less, earn more; pay more, earn less. Take the company's current per share earnings and divide it by the current price of a single share. This will give you the investment's initial rate of return. Then compare the investment's initial rate of return and expected growth rate per share to the return being paid on U.S. treasury bonds. If the treasuries look juicier, the stock might be overpriced.

To establish the value of the company relative to treasury bonds, divide the current per share earnings by the current return on treasury bonds. Relative Value = Per Share Earnings / Current Treasury Bond Return.

points.title: Projected annual compounding return as an equity/bond (Book Value model)
points.question: What is the company's projected annual compounding return as an equity/bond? Take the company's average per share return on equity for the last ten years and subtract the average percentage that is not retained and is paid out as a dividend. Use the resulting difference as the rate of growth that the company's book value will grow. Use the company's book value in the current year as the present value (PV), and use the calculated rate of growth for book value as the rate of interest (i). Punch in 10 for the number of years out that you want to make your projection (N), then hit the CPT key, followed by the future-value key (FV). This will calculate the per share book value of the company ten years out. To determine the selling price of the company's stock ten years out, take the company's future per share book value and multiply it by the average return on equity - this gives the company's projected per share earnings. Then multiply the projected earnings by the company's average annual P/E ratio for the last ten years - this gives the company's projected per share future trading price. Using the company's current market price as your present value (PV) and the projected future trading price as the future value (FV) and the number of years between the two (N), hit CPT and then the i key, which calculates the projected annual compounding return that the investment will produce.

points.title: Projected return using historical per-share earnings growth / Intrinsic Value
points.question: What is the projected annual compounding return using the historical annual per share earnings growth? To calculate the projected annual compounding return on an investment purchased in 2002 and sold during 2012, first determine the annual compounding per share growth from 1992 to 2002. Then, using the 1992 to 2002 per share growth rate, project forward the company's per share earnings to 2012 and multiply it by the average annual P/E ratio for 1992 to 2002. This will give you the projected trading price of the stock in 2012. Use the 1992 per share earnings as the present value (PV), 2002 per share earnings as the future value (FV) and 10 for the number of years (N), hit CPT and the i key to get the company's per share annual compounding growth rate. Now use the 2002 per share earnings as PV, that growth rate as i, and 10 years - hit CPT then FV - to get the projected per share earnings for 2012. Multiply by the average P/E ratio to get the projected trading price.

If you can't find a durable competitive advantage, keep your powder dry until you do. Waiting for the perfect pitch never bothered Warren.

points.title: Brand-name product or key service
points.question: Does the company have a brand name product or service that gives it a competitive advantage? If 6, 7, 5.2, 8 are a yes, then you need to find out whether it is selling a product or service that has a durable competitive advantage. Does it sell a brand-name product or a key service that people or businesses are dependent on? Products are much easier to identify than services, so start with them. Ask yourself: Is the product the kind that stores have to carry to be in business? Would the businesses that carry this kind of product be losing sales if they didn't carry this particular brand-name product? If you remember your parents using it, drinking it, smoking it or doing something else with it, it is usually a good sign. Ask a pharmacist or a car mechanic - related people - they can tell how it sold and how it sells. Better if it's a CRAP. Companies providing services that have durable competitive advantages are much harder to identify. Look to the economics of the business: is the company's service necessary for businesses that use it to stay in business? If the service is aimed at individual consumers, ask whether consumers are constantly in need of it. As in the world of products, the frequency of the consumer's need differentiates the quality of the competitive advantage.

points.title: Earnings-per-share growth-rate test (5 year vs 10 year)
points.question: A test for determining the earnings per share growth rate. For earnings to grow, the company must employ its retained earnings in a manner that will generate more earnings per share. The increase in per share earnings will, over time, increase the price of the share. Mathematical method: figure the annual compounded rate of growth of per share earnings for the last ten years (long term) and the last five years (short term). If, for example, long term is 12% and short term is 16%, the company has had a higher rate of return of earnings growth in the last five years than in the ten year period. What were the business economics that caused this change? Is the company buying up its stock? Finding new business ventures? Note: to adapt the per share growth rate to negative earnings, simply start back one year. You should never use fewer than seven years.

points.title: Actively buying back its shares
points.question: Is the company actively buying back its shares? The repurchasing of shares is one of Warren's favourite tricks to increase his ownership in a company without having to invest any more of his own money. Take the number of shares outstanding ten years ago, subtract from it the number of shares outstanding in the current year, and you get the number of shares the company has purchased over the last ten years. A negative number indicates the number of shares that the company has added. Warren is looking for a decrease in the number of shares outstanding.

points.title: Can the company repurchase shares to investors' advantage?
points.question: A good sign that a company has a DCA is that it will have a long history of buying back its shares. To buy back shares over a number of years, a company needs an abundance of free cash. Companies with DCA have the economic power to earn the money they need to implement a long term share repurchase programme. Price competitive businesses seldom have the excess capital necessary to buy back shares. Instead the reverse happens: they issue more shares to raise new money to support their cash hungry businesses.

points.title: Can the company increase prices along with inflation?
points.question: Can the company increase prices along with inflation? It might not be a great wealth building tool, but a company with a DCA offers an increase in value right along with inflation. An interesting question that requires investigative work. If the company's product is selling at the same price as twenty years ago, then you are most likely dealing with a commodity business and should give it a pass. If the price of the product has risen on an average of at least 4% a year over the last twenty years, then you can bet the farm that it's the kind of business that can raise prices along with inflation. Financial equation for use with TI BA-35 Solar calculator: company's ability to raise prices with inflation. Use the price of the product twenty years ago as your present value (PV), the current price of the product as your future value (FV), and 20 as your number of years (N). Hit compute (CPT) then the interest key (i) and your annual compounding growth rate in price will be calculated. (If you get a negative number, it means you are probably looking at a price-competitive business and should move on.)

points.title: Right operational costs (low maintenance capex)
points.question: Does the company have right operational costs? The more durable a competitive advantage, the less a business has to spend to maintain it. A simple mathematical formula is to take the amount of earnings retained by a business for a certain period and measure its effect on the earning capacity of the company. With DCA, retained earnings are either used to expand operations, invest in new businesses and/or repurchases - all three should have a positive effect on per share earnings. Are large capital expenditures required to update plant and equipment? If they are building cars or designing software, they may not have to buy big expensive jets, or can use the same equipment for twenty years without any risk of obsolescence. If the answer is yes, be careful.

points.title: Market panic, business recession or curable individual calamity
points.question: Is the company's stock price suffering from a market panic, a business recession, or an individual calamity that is curable? As we discussed, these types of situations usually offer the best prices. If you can't buy during one of these events, then you are probably paying full price for the stock. If you want to get rich, you have to learn how to exploit a bad-news situation and the stock market's shortsightedness.

points.title: Initial rate of return vs US Treasury bonds
points.question: What is the initial rate of return on the investment and how does it compare to the return on U.S. treasury bonds? The price you pay to BUY determines your rate of return - pay less, earn more; pay more, earn less. Take the company's current per share earnings and divide it by the current price of a single share. This will give you the investment's initial rate of return. Then compare the investment's initial rate of return and expected growth rate per share to the return being paid on U.S. treasury bonds. If the treasuries look juicier, the stock might be overpriced.

points.title: Stock's value relative to Treasury bonds
points.question: A stock's value relative to treasury bonds: all investments compete with one another but the return on treasury bonds is the benchmark that all investments must ultimately compete with. To establish the value of the company relative to treasury bonds, divide the current per share earnings by the current return on treasury bonds. Relative Value = Per Share Earnings / Current Treasury Bond Return.

points.title: Projected annual compounding return as an equity/bond (Book Value model)
points.question: What is the company's projected annual compounding return as an equity/bond? Take the company's average per share return on equity for the last ten years and subtract the average percentage that is not retained and is paid out as a dividend. Use the resulting difference as the rate of growth that the company's book value will grow. Use the company's book value in the current year as the present value (PV), and use the calculated rate of growth for book value as the rate of interest (i). Punch in 10 for the number of years out that you want to make your projection (N), then hit the CPT key, followed by the future-value key (FV). This will calculate the per share book value of the company ten years out. To determine the selling price of the company's stock ten years out, take the company's future per share book value and multiply it by the average return on equity - this gives the company's projected per share earnings. Then multiply the projected earnings by the company's average annual P/E ratio for the last ten years - this gives the company's projected per share future trading price. Using the company's current market price as your present value (PV) and the projected future trading price as the future value (FV) and the number of years between the two (N), hit CPT and then the i key, which calculates the projected annual compounding return that the investment will produce.

points.title: Projected return using historical per-share earnings growth / Intrinsic Value
points.question: What is the projected annual compounding return using the historical annual per share earnings growth? To calculate the projected annual compounding return on an investment purchased in 2002 and sold during 2012, first determine the annual compounding per share growth from 1992 to 2002. Then, using the 1992 to 2002 per share growth rate, project forward the company's per share earnings to 2012 and multiply it by the average annual P/E ratio for 1992 to 2002. This will give you the projected trading price of the stock in 2012. Use the 1992 per share earnings as the present value (PV), 2002 per share earnings as the future value (FV) and 10 for the number of years (N), hit CPT and the i key to get the company's per share annual compounding growth rate. Now use the 2002 per share earnings as PV, that growth rate as i, and 10 years - hit CPT then FV - to get the projected per share earnings for 2012. Multiply by the average P/E ratio to get the projected trading price.

points.title: Brand-name product or key service
points.question: Does the company have a brand name product or service that gives it a competitive advantage? If 6, 7, 5.2, 8 are a yes, then you need to find out whether it is selling a product or service that has a durable competitive advantage. Does it sell a brand-name product or a key service that people or businesses are dependent on? Products are much easier to identify than services, so start with them. Ask yourself: Is the product the kind that stores have to carry to be in business? Would the businesses that carry this kind of product be losing sales if they didn't carry this particular brand-name product? If you remember your parents using it, drinking it, smoking it or doing something else with it, it is usually a good sign. points.title: Predicting earnings at a glance (Company I / II / III / IV)
points.question: One will confront four types of companies, among them three interest us. Company 3: shows a substantially weaker performance in the latest year than the year before. Company 4: shows an actual loss. Is the condition permanent or is it something that management or the economic environment can correct over time?

points.title: Earnings-per-share growth-rate test (5 year vs 10 year)
points.question: A test for determining the earnings per share growth rate. For earnings to grow, the company must employ its retained earnings in a manner that will generate more earnings per share. The increase in per share earnings will, over time, increase the price of the share. Mathematical method: figure the annual compounded rate of growth of per share earnings for the last ten years (long term) and the last five years (short term). If, for example, long term is 12% and short term is 16%, the company has had a higher rate of return of earnings growth in the last five years than in the ten year period. What were the business economics that caused this change? Is the company buying up its stock? Finding new business ventures? Note: to adapt the per share growth rate to negative earnings, simply start back one year. You should never use fewer than seven years.

points.title: Actively buying back its shares
points.question: Is the company actively buying back its shares? The repurchasing of shares is one of Warren's favourite tricks to increase his ownership in a company without having to invest any more of his own money. Take the number of shares outstanding ten years ago, subtract from it the number of shares outstanding in the current year, and you get the number of shares the company has purchased over the last ten years. A negative number indicates the number of shares that the company has added. Warren is looking for a decrease in the number of shares outstanding.

points.title: Can the company repurchase shares to investors' advantage?
points.question: A good sign that a company has a DCA is that it will have a long history of buying back its shares. To buy back shares over a number of years, a company needs an abundance of free cash. Companies with DCA have the economic power to earn the money they need to implement a long term share repurchase programme. Price competitive businesses seldom have the excess capital necessary to buy back shares. Instead the reverse happens: they issue more shares to raise new money to support their cash hungry businesses.

points.title: Can the company increase prices along with inflation?
points.question: Can the company increase prices along with inflation? It might not be a great wealth building tool, but a company with a DCA offers an increase in value right along with inflation. An interesting question that requires investigative work. If the company's product is selling at the same price as twenty years ago, then you are most likely dealing with a commodity business and should give it a pass. If the price of the product has risen on an average of at least 4% a year over the last twenty years, then you can bet the farm that it's the kind of business that can raise prices along with inflation. Financial equation for use with TI BA-35 Solar calculator: company's ability to raise prices with inflation. Use the price of the product twenty years ago as your present value (PV), the current price of the product as your future value (FV), and 20 as your number of years (N). Hit compute (CPT) then the interest key (i) and your annual compounding growth rate in price will be calculated. (If you get a negative number, it means you are probably looking at a price-competitive business and should move on.)

points.title: Right operational costs (low maintenance capex)
points.question: Does the company have right operational costs? The more durable a competitive advantage, the less a business has to spend to maintain it. A simple mathematical formula is to take the amount of earnings retained by a business for a certain period and measure its effect on the earning capacity of the company. With DCA, retained earnings are either used to expand operations, invest in new businesses and/or repurchases - all three should have a positive effect on per share earnings. Are large capital expenditures required to update plant and equipment? If they are building cars or designing software, they may not have to buy big expensive jets, or can use the same equipment for twenty years without any risk of obsolescence. If the answer is yes, be careful.

points.question: Is the company's stock price suffering from a market panic, a business recession, or an individual calamity that is curable? As we discussed, these types of situations usually offer the best prices. If you can't buy during one of these events, then you are probably paying full price for the stock. If you want to get rich, you have to learn how to exploit a bad-news situation and the stock market's shortsightedness.

points.title: Initial rate of return vs US Treasury bonds
points.question: What is the initial rate of return on the investment and how does it compare to the return on U.S. treasury bonds? The price you pay to BUY determines your rate of return - pay less, earn more; pay more, earn less. Take the company's current per share earnings and divide it by the current price of a single share. This will give you the investment's initial rate of return. Then compare the investment's initial rate of return and expected growth rate per share to the return being paid on U.S. treasury bonds. If the treasuries look juicier, the stock might be overpriced.

points.title: Stock's value relative to Treasury bonds
points.question: A stock's value relative to treasury bonds: all investments compete with one another but the return on treasury bonds is the benchmark that all investments must ultimately compete with. To establish the value of the company relative to treasury bonds, divide the current per share earnings by the current return on treasury bonds. Relative Value = Per Share Earnings / Current Treasury Bond Return.

points.title: Projected annual compounding return as an equity/bond (Book Value model)
points.question: What is the company's projected annual compounding return as an equity/bond? Take the company's average per share return on equity for the last ten years and subtract the average percentage that is not retained and is paid out as a dividend. Use the resulting difference as the rate of growth that the company's book value will grow. Use the company's book value in the current year as the present value (PV), and use the calculated rate of growth for book value as the rate of interest (i). Punch in 10 for the number of years out that you want to make your projection (N), then hit the CPT key, followed by the future-value key (FV). This will calculate the per share book value of the company ten years out. To determine the selling price of the company's stock ten years out, take the company's future per share book value and multiply it by the average return on equity - this gives the company's projected per share earnings. Then multiply the projected earnings by the company's average annual P/E ratio for the last ten years - this gives the company's projected per share future trading price. Using the company's current market price as your present value (PV) and the projected future trading price as the future value (FV) and the number of years between the two (N), hit CPT and then the i key, which calculates the projected annual compounding return that the investment will produce.

Using the company's current market price as your present value (PV) and the projected future trading price as the future value (FV) and the number of years between the two (N), hit CPT and then the i key, which calculates the projected annual compounding return that the investment will produce.

points.question: What is the projected annual compounding return using the historical annual per share earnings growth? To calculate the projected annual compounding return on an investment purchased in 2002 and sold during 2012, first determine the annual compounding per share growth from 1992 to 2002. Then, using the 1992 to 2002 per share growth rate, project forward the company's per share earnings to 2012 and multiply it by the average annual P/E ratio for 1992 to 2002. Now use the 2002 per share earnings as PV, that growth rate as i, and 10 years - hit CPT then FV - to get the projected per share earnings for 2012. Multiply by the average P/E ratio to get the projected trading price.

points.title: Brand-name product or key service
points.question: Does the company have a brand name product or service that gives it a competitive advantage? If 6, 7, 5.2, 8 are a yes, then you need to find out whether it is selling a product or service that has a durable competitive advantage. Does it sell a brand-name product or a key service that people or businesses are dependent on? Products are much easier to identify than services, so start with them. Ask yourself: Is the product the kind that stores have to carry to be in business? Would the businesses that carry this kind of product be losing sales if they didn't carry this particular brand-name product? If you remember your parents using it, drinking it, smoking it or doing something else with it, it is usually a good sign. Ask a pharmacist or a car mechanic - related people - they can tell how it sold and how it sells. Better if it's a CRAP. Companies providing services that have durable competitive advantages are much harder to identify. Look to the economics of the business: is the company's service necessary for businesses that use it to stay in business? If the service is aimed at individual consumers, ask whether consumers are constantly in need of it. As in the world of products, the frequency of the consumer's need differentiates the quality of the competitive advantage.

points.title: Predicting earnings at a glance (Company I / II / III / IV)
points.question: One will confront four types of companies, among them three interest us. Company 1: in a perfect situation, a company's per share earnings are consistently A) Strong and B) Show an upward trend. Is the condition permanent or is it something that management or the economic environment can correct over time?

points.title: Earnings-per-share growth-rate test (5 year vs 10 year)
points.question: A test for determining the earnings per share growth rate. For earnings to grow, the company must employ its retained earnings in a manner that will generate more earnings per share. The increase in per share earnings will, over time, increase the price of the share. Mathematical method: figure the annual compounded rate of growth of per share earnings for the last ten years (long term) and the last five years (short term). If, for example, long term is 12% and short term is 16%, the company has had a higher rate of return of earnings growth in the last five years than in the ten year period. What were the business economics that caused this change? Is the company buying up its stock? Finding new business ventures? Note: to adapt the per share growth rate to negative earnings, simply start back one year. You should never use fewer than seven years.

points.title: Actively buying back its shares
points.question: Is the company actively buying back its shares? The repurchasing of shares is one of Warren's favourite tricks to increase his ownership in a company without having to invest any more of his own money. Take the number of shares outstanding ten years ago, subtract from it the number of shares outstanding in the current year, and you get the number of shares the company has purchased over the last ten years. A negative number indicates the number of shares that the company has added. Warren is looking for a decrease in the number of shares outstanding.

points.title: Can the company repurchase shares to investors' advantage?
points.question: A good sign that a company has a DCA is that it will have a long history of buying back its shares. To buy back shares over a number of years, a company needs an abundance of free cash. Companies with DCA have the economic power to earn the money they need to implement a long term share repurchase programme. Price competitive businesses seldom have the excess capital necessary to buy back shares. Instead the reverse happens: they issue more shares to raise new money to support their cash hungry businesses.

points.title: Can the company increase prices along with inflation?
points.question: Can the company increase prices along with inflation? It might not be a great wealth building tool, but a company with a DCA offers an increase in value right along with inflation. An interesting question that requires investigative work. If the company's product is selling at the same price as twenty years ago, then you are most likely dealing with a commodity business and should give it a pass. If the price of the product has risen on an average of at least 4% a year over the last twenty years, then you can bet the farm that it's the kind of business that can raise prices along with inflation. Financial equation for use with TI BA-35 Solar calculator: company's ability to raise prices with inflation. Use the price of the product twenty years ago as your present value (PV), the current price of the product as your future value (FV), and 20 as your number of years (N). Hit compute (CPT) then the interest key (i) and your annual compounding growth rate in price will be calculated. (If you get a negative number, it means you are probably looking at a price-competitive business and should move on.)

points.title: Right operational costs (low maintenance capex)
points.question: Does the company have right operational costs? The more durable a competitive advantage, the less a business has to spend to maintain it. A simple mathematical formula is to take the amount of earnings retained by a business for a certain period and measure its effect on the earning capacity of the company. With DCA, retained earnings are either used to expand operations, invest in new businesses and/or repurchases - all three should have a positive effect on per share earnings. Are large capital expenditures required to update plant and equipment? If they are building cars or designing software, they may not have to buy big expensive jets, or can use the same equipment for twenty years without any risk of obsolescence. If the answer is yes, be careful.

With DCA, retained earnings are either used to expand operations, invest in new businesses and/or repurchases - all three should have a positive effect on per share earnings. Are large capital expenditures required to update plant and equipment? If they are building cars or designing software, they may not have to buy big expensive jets, or can use the same equipment for twenty years without any risk of obsolescence. If the answer is yes, be careful.

points.title: Market panic, business recession or curable individual calamity
points.question: Is the company's stock price suffering from a market panic, a business recession, or an individual calamity that is curable? As we discussed, these types of situations usually offer the best prices. If you can't buy during one of these events, then you are probably paying full price for the stock. If you want to get rich, you have to learn how to exploit a bad-news situation and the stock market's shortsightedness.

points.title: Initial rate of return vs US Treasury bonds
points.question: What is the initial rate of return on the investment and how does it compare to the return on U.S. treasury bonds? The price you pay to BUY determines your rate of return - pay less, earn more; pay more, earn less. Take the company's current per share earnings and divide it by the current price of a single share. This will give you the investment's initial rate of return. Then compare the investment's initial rate of return and expected growth rate per share to the return being paid on U.S. treasury bonds. If the treasuries look juicier, the stock might be overpriced.

To establish the value of the company relative to treasury bonds, divide the current per share earnings by the current return on treasury bonds. Relative Value = Per Share Earnings / Current Treasury Bond Return.

points.title: Projected annual compounding return as an equity/bond (Book Value model)
points.question: What is the company's projected annual compounding return as an equity/bond? Take the company's average per share return on equity for the last ten years and subtract the average percentage that is not retained and is paid out as a dividend. Use the resulting difference as the rate of growth that the company's book value will grow. Use the company's book value in the current year as the present value (PV), and use the calculated rate of growth for book value as the rate of interest (i). Punch in 10 for the number of years out that you want to make your projection (N), then hit the CPT key, followed by the future-value key (FV). This will calculate the per share book value of the company ten years out. To determine the selling price of the company's stock ten years out, take the company's future per share book value and multiply it by the average return on equity - this gives the company's projected per share earnings. Then multiply the projected earnings by the company's average annual P/E ratio for the last ten years - this gives the company's projected per share future trading price. Using the company's current market price as your present value (PV) and the projected future trading price as the future value (FV) and the number of years between the two (N), hit CPT and then the i key, which calculates the projected annual compounding return that the investment will produce.
